print((out/'manuscript.txt').read_text()[:55000])
PY"

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer vision problem: jointly handling forgetting, class imbalance, and unknown classes in continual semantic segmentation. Maintaining multiple unknown clusters and learning their assignments is a plausible improvement over collapsing all unknown pixels into one background representation.

The empirical evaluation is substantial, covering three datasets, multiple incremental schedules, and CNN and Transformer architectures. With DeepLab-V3, FALCON improves over FairCL from 37.0 to 37.9 mIoU on ADE20K 100-50 and from 34.7 to 36.4 on ADE20K 100-10. Cityscapes 1-1 improves from 49.22 to 55.24.

The ablations provide meaningful evidence of component usefulness. In Table 1, replacing vanilla contrastive clustering increases minority-class mIoU from 26.4 to 30.8 on ADE20K 100-50 while also improving majority-class performance. Table 2 supports updating the visual grammar model rather than keeping its ImageNet initialization fixed.

The framework figures and training algorithm communicate the overall procedure clearly. The appendix supplies several implementation details and sensitivity studies for the scaling factor, cluster margin, neighborhood size, and backbone.
weaknesses: The central fairness interpretation does not follow from Propositions 1–2. These propositions characterize normalized softmax weights, not feature compactness or segmentation fairness. A weight of 1/L changes when samples are duplicated without any change in cluster geometry. Consequently, reducing differences between these weights does not establish the claimed reduction in minority-class feature scatter. This is a substantive gap in the paper's main theoretical justification.

The objective and optimization contain consequential inconsistencies. Proposition 2 requires the transition vector v to participate in the softmax normalizer, but Eq. (4) does not explicitly include it; under the stated pixel-feature normalizer, increasing v·c makes its loss term unbounded below. Separately, Eq. (8) optimizes segmentation parameters while the cluster regularizer depends only on prototypes described as fixed during loss computation and updated by momentum. No gradient path explaining how this regularizer changes the segmentation model is specified, despite the gains attributed to it in Table 4.

The claimed distillation upper bound in Appendix Section 4 is unsupported. The derivation assumes a metric satisfying the triangle inequality, then identifies its terms with the contrastive objective without establishing that equivalence. The subsequent Big-O manipulation also does not establish the claimed pointwise upper bound or preservation of previous knowledge.

The ablations do not fully isolate the proposed mechanisms. In Table 4, removing visual grammar also reduces the number of unknown clusters to one, confounding learned assignment with the benefit of multiple clusters. A comparison using the same multiple clusters with nearest-centroid assignment is needed. Likewise, comparisons against the cited balanced or parametric contrastive alternatives would clarify the contribution beyond adapting existing loss and clustering designs.

Material reproducibility details remain missing: how unknown pixels are selected when old and future classes share the background label; how conflicting cluster assignments are resolved; how unknown cluster identities enter cross-entropy pseudo-labels; DBSCAN parameters; and the visual grammar pretraining and training schedules. These omissions affect implementation of the central method, rather than merely presentation.

The consistent empirical gains make this a worthwhile submission, but the unresolved objective, optimization, and theoretical issues currently favor Weak Reject. Secondary reservations include the absence of runtime or memory measurements supporting efficiency claims and the fact that the advertised 8.0-point improvement over CoMFormer compares different segmentation architectures, although the matched-architecture comparisons also show improvements.
